title: Football regulator will be ‘positive’ for investment, chief executive says
content:
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will make the English game more attractive to investors, raise ownership standards and drive down borrowing costs for clubs, according to its new chief executive Richard Monks.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, the former Financial Conduct Authority director rejected the idea that English football’s regulatory experiment will scare off potential new owners, endangering clubs and depriving the game of fresh energy, funding and ideas.

“Put yourself in an investor’s shoes,” said Monks, who was appointed as IFR CEO in September after 21 years with the UK’s regulator for the financial services industry.

“Would you want to invest in a club that has proper financial plans, clarity about how they’re funded and robust plans in place in case things go wrong? I think if you’re an investor, you’d want this.

“It’s a positive for investment and our regime is just common sense. I think it will attract the right sort of investment, as opposed to turning off investment. In terms of the cost of complying with this, it will be very small.

“This could be a very different regime, where the IFR is restricting clubs’ expenditure, but we’re absolutely not doing that. What we’re saying is, ‘if you want to spend, you can go ahead and do that’, but we need to make sure the club is protected because that investment could dry up.

“I actually think that’s a positive message to investors and the engagement we’re doing with clubs would, so far, back that up.”

The argument that the IFR could make it harder for incumbent owners to sell their clubs has been made repeatedly in recent years by opponents of statutory regulation, with West Ham United vice-chair Karren Brady and Crystal Palace co-owner Steve Parish among the more vocal critics of the idea.

However, the creation of an independent regulator has been a strong possibility ever since it was recommended in former sports minister Dame Tracey Crouch’s Fan-Led Review in 2022, with draft legislation first proposed two years ago. Over that period, there have been full takeovers or minority investments at seven of the 20 teams currently in the Premier League, including two since the IFR was formally created last summer, with more than a dozen deals done in the English Football League (EFL) over the same time span.

Monks also believes that regulation should drive down football’s borrowing costs, which have been high for years as a result of most banks refusing to lend money to football clubs because of their chronic losses and strained balance sheets. This has led many clubs to rely on the equivalent of pay-day loans, a practice that has compounded their financial problems.

“A well-regulated industry, where clubs have clear financial plans and stress tests are in place, may make it easier for creditors to lend to football clubs with the confidence that some crisis is not about to occur that will drive them over the cliff edge,” he said.

Monks was speaking on the day that the IFR launched a second consultation period for its proposed licensing regime, the system that will underpin its core mission to make clubs in the top five divisions of English men’s football more sustainable and financially resilient.

From the start of the 2027-28 season, the 116 clubs in scope will need a licence to compete. The first step will be an application for a provisional licence, which will be granted once a club publishes basic information about its owners and senior executives, as well as a business plan for that season.

A full licence, which lasts for three years, will be awarded once the club has met four mandatory licence conditions: a more detailed business plan, which addresses common risk factors; a report on how the club proposes to meet the IFR’s club governance code, including actions it will take to improve equality, diversity and inclusion; proof the club is properly consulting its fans; and an annual declaration of compliance with the rules.

Furthermore, clubs will have to ensure that they have sufficient resources, including cash in the bank for rainy days, enough qualified staff to operate and the required physical assets — a safe stadium, for example — to function as a professional outfit.

However, Monks pointed out that the licensing regime would be flexible, proportionate and risk-based. So, well-run clubs that do not lose money and have great balance sheets will be treated differently to poorly-run clubs that are haemorrhaging cash and have few assets.

Monks is confident that there should be fewer of the latter going forward, as the IFR’s team of supervisors, or “relationship managers”, should be able to “course correct” clubs in difficulty before the situation becomes critical.

“The IFR will work with clubs and support them to meet the licensing requirements which are absolutely essential to our mission to change English football for good,” he said.

“The regulatory regime will focus on financial reality not accounting presentation, including the amount of cash the club will be required to hold.

“If the IFR believes a club is at risk of failing to meet the necessary requirements, the regulator may impose specific licence conditions to get clubs back on track. Depending on the risk posed, this may require clubs holding a sufficient level of liquidity, reducing expenditure, or restructuring debt.”

This consultation window is open for seven weeks. The IFR will then publish the final licensing rules and guidance in July, before starting a pilot scheme with a small number of volunteer clubs to test the regime.

In the meantime, the regulator has also written to all club in the top five divisions to ask if they are currently in talks with new investors to make sure the IFR is ready to take responsibility for approving new owners, directors and senior executives from the leagues in May. Monks explained that the IFR has been talking to Sheffield Wednesday’s administrators and the EFL for several months to make sure all relevant parties are aware of what is expected going forward.

Later this year, it will also start the consultation period on the mandatory levy that the clubs must pay to fund the IFR. It is expected Premier League clubs will pay the greatest share.
